subject: math
cluster: Draw, construct, and describe geometrical figures and describe the relationships between them
skillName: Drawing Geometric Shapes with Given Conditions
intro: Classify each set of conditions as determining a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle, and name the governing criterion (SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, or AAA) when one applies. Remember: SSS, SAS, ASA, and AAA name three matched parts, the included angle in SAS must sit between the two given sides, and three angles alone (AAA) fix the shape but not the size.

items.prompt: A triangle is given by two sides of $6\text{ cm}$ and $9\text{ cm}$ with an included angle of $50^\circ$ between them. Does this determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle? Name the criterion.

steps: Identify the given parts: two sides ($6\text{ cm}$ and $9\text{ cm}$) and the angle between them ($50^\circ$).
Because the angle lies between the two given sides, this is the side-angle-side pattern, SAS.
SAS fixes the shape and the size of the triangle, so exactly one triangle can be drawn.
Answer: a unique triangle, by SAS.

items.prompt: A triangle has two angles of $40^\circ$ and $75^\circ$ with an included side of $8\text{ cm}$ between those two angles. Does this determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle? Name the criterion.

steps: The given parts are two angles ($40^\circ$ and $75^\circ$) and the side that lies between them ($8\text{ cm}$).
An angle, the side between the two angles, then the second angle is the angle-side-angle pattern, ASA.
ASA determines a unique triangle.
Check feasibility: the third angle is $180^\circ - 40^\circ - 75^\circ = 65^\circ$, which is positive, so the triangle exists.
Answer: a unique triangle, by ASA.

items.prompt: A triangle is described only by its three angle measures: $45^\circ$, $60^\circ$, and $75^\circ$, with no side length given. Does this determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle? Name the criterion.
items.answer: More than one triangle (infinitely many similar triangles), by AAA.

steps: First check that the angles can form a triangle: $45^\circ + 60^\circ + 75^\circ = 180^\circ$, so they are valid.
Three angles with no side length is the AAA pattern.
AAA fixes the shape of the triangle but not its size, because every enlargement or reduction keeps the same angles.
So infinitely many similar triangles satisfy the conditions.
Answer: more than one triangle (infinitely many similar triangles), by AAA.

items.prompt: A triangle is given by three side lengths: $5\text{ cm}$, $7\text{ cm}$, and $9\text{ cm}$. Does this determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle? Name the criterion.

steps: Test the triangle inequality on the two shorter sides against the longest: $5 + 7 = 12 > 9$.
Since the two shorter sides sum to more than the longest side, a triangle can be formed.
Three given side lengths is the side-side-side pattern, SSS.
SSS determines a unique triangle.
Answer: a unique triangle, by SSS.

items.prompt: A triangle is given by angles of $35^\circ$ and $80^\circ$ and a side of $10\text{ cm}$ that lies opposite the $35^\circ$ angle (not between the two angles). Does this determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle? Name the criterion.

steps: The given parts are two angles ($35^\circ$ and $80^\circ$) and a non-included side ($10\text{ cm}$).
Two angles and a side that is not between them is the angle-angle-side pattern, AAS.
Once two angles are known, the third angle is fixed at $180^\circ - 35^\circ - 80^\circ = 65^\circ$, so the shape is set and the one given side fixes the size.
AAS determines a unique triangle.
Answer: a unique triangle, by AAS.

items.prompt: A triangle is to be built from side lengths $3\text{ cm}$, $4\text{ cm}$, and $7\text{ cm}$. Does this determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle? Explain using the triangle inequality.

steps: Add the two shorter sides and compare to the longest: $3 + 4 = 7$.
The sum equals the longest side exactly rather than exceeding it.
When the two shorter sides only just reach the longest side, the figure collapses into a straight segment, so no actual triangle forms.
Answer: no triangle (this is the degenerate boundary case).

items.prompt: A triangle is given by two sides of $5\text{ cm}$ and $12\text{ cm}$ with an included angle of $90^\circ$ between them. Does this determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle? Name the criterion.

steps: The given parts are two sides ($5\text{ cm}$ and $12\text{ cm}$) and the angle between them ($90^\circ$).
An angle located between the two given sides is the side-angle-side pattern, SAS.
SAS determines a unique triangle.
Answer: a unique triangle, by SAS.

items.prompt: A triangle is described by two angles of $60^\circ$ and $120^\circ$ with an included side of $9\text{ cm}$ between them. Does this determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle? Explain.

steps: The pattern looks like ASA, but first check that the two given angles can belong to a triangle.
Add the two angles: $60^\circ + 120^\circ = 180^\circ$.
Two angles already use the full $180^\circ$, leaving $180^\circ - 180^\circ = 0^\circ$ for the third angle.
A triangle cannot have a $0^\circ$ angle, so no triangle can be formed.
Answer: no triangle.

items.prompt: Using a ruler and protractor, you are asked to construct a triangle with a $7\text{ cm}$ base, a $50^\circ$ angle at one end of the base, and a $65^\circ$ angle at the other end. Will every student's triangle be the same? State the criterion that applies.
items.answer: Yes, a unique triangle, by ASA.

steps: Draw the $7\text{ cm}$ base, then use the protractor to draw a $50^\circ$ angle at one endpoint and a $65^\circ$ angle at the other endpoint.
The two rays from the endpoints meet at exactly one point, forming the third vertex.
The given parts are an angle, the included side, and another angle, which is the ASA pattern.
Check feasibility: the third angle is $180^\circ - 50^\circ - 65^\circ = 65^\circ$, which is positive, so the triangle exists.
ASA gives a unique triangle, so every correctly drawn triangle is congruent.
Answer: yes, a unique triangle, by ASA.

items.prompt: A triangle is given by two sides of $8\text{ cm}$ and $5\text{ cm}$ and an angle of $40^\circ$ that is opposite the $5\text{ cm}$ side (the angle is not between the two given sides). Which congruence pattern is named by these parts, and does that pattern guarantee a unique triangle? Name the pattern.
items.answer: The pattern is SSA, which does not guarantee a unique triangle.

steps: List the parts: two sides ($8\text{ cm}$ and $5\text{ cm}$) and an angle that is not between them, opposite the $5\text{ cm}$ side.
Two sides and a non-included angle is the side-side-angle pattern, SSA.
SSA is the ambiguous case: unlike SAS, it does not by itself fix the triangle, so it is not one of the criteria that always give a unique triangle.
Answer: the pattern is SSA, which does not guarantee a unique triangle.

items.prompt: A triangle is given by side lengths $6\text{ cm}$, $6\text{ cm}$, and $13\text{ cm}$. Does this determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle? Justify with the triangle inequality.

steps: Add the two shorter sides and compare to the longest: $6 + 6 = 12$.
Compare to the longest side: $12 < 13$.
Because the two shorter sides together are less than the longest side, they cannot reach across to close the triangle.
Answer: no triangle.

items.prompt: A triangle is given by an angle of $30^\circ$ between two sides of $10\text{ cm}$ and $10\text{ cm}$. Does this determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle? Name the criterion.

steps: The given parts are two sides ($10\text{ cm}$ and $10\text{ cm}$) with the $30^\circ$ angle between them.
An angle between two given sides is the side-angle-side pattern, SAS.
SAS determines a unique triangle (here an isosceles triangle).
Answer: a unique triangle, by SAS.

items.prompt: A triangle is described by three angle measures: $90^\circ$, $45^\circ$, and $45^\circ$, with no side length given. Does this determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle? Name the criterion.
items.answer: More than one triangle (infinitely many similar triangles), by AAA.

steps: Check the angle sum: $90^\circ + 45^\circ + 45^\circ = 180^\circ$, so the angles are valid.
Three angles with no side is the AAA pattern.
AAA fixes the shape but not the size, so any scaled copy of the triangle also fits.
Therefore infinitely many similar triangles satisfy the conditions.
Answer: more than one triangle (infinitely many similar triangles), by AAA.

items.prompt: Draw a quadrilateral that has exactly one pair of parallel sides and contains two right angles. Name the figure, and state whether the four given conditions (one pair of parallel sides plus two right angles) by themselves fix a single size of figure.
items.answer: A right trapezoid; no, the conditions do not fix a single size.

steps: A quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides is a trapezoid.
Placing two right angles along one of the non-parallel sides makes that side perpendicular to both parallel sides.
A trapezoid with a right angle (in fact two adjacent right angles) is called a right trapezoid.
Because no specific side lengths are given, many right trapezoids of different sizes meet the conditions, so the figure is not fixed to one size.
Answer: a right trapezoid; the conditions do not determine a single size.

items.prompt: Two students compare triangles. One drew a triangle from angles $50^\circ$, $60^\circ$, $70^\circ$ (no side given); the other drew a triangle from a $50^\circ$ angle included between sides of $4\text{ cm}$ and $6\text{ cm}$. For each set of conditions, state whether it determines a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle, and name the criterion.
items.answer: First set: more than one triangle, by AAA. Second set: a unique triangle, by SAS.

steps: First set: the angles sum to $50^\circ + 60^\circ + 70^\circ = 180^\circ$, so they are valid, but with no side length the AAA pattern fixes only the shape, giving infinitely many similar triangles.
So the first set determines more than one triangle, by AAA.
Second set: two sides ($4\text{ cm}$ and $6\text{ cm}$) with the angle between them ($50^\circ$) is the SAS pattern.
SAS fixes both shape and size, so it determines a unique triangle.
Answer: first set, more than one triangle by AAA; second set, a unique triangle by SAS.
